articles.headline: Our Black Hills Trip
articles.text:
[The following is a rather hap-hazard jotting down of the incidents in the first part of our Black Hills trip. The next issue will contain a longer and probably more interesting article on the resources of the Hills.]

We left the Medora brick-yard at 5 o'clock Monday afternoon in a buck-board barouche, drawn by a pair of Pennell & Roberts' mules and driven by a Spanish nobleman, disgnised under the name of Patrick Devlin. The party consisted of P. D. Cravath, an old college friend, the afore-mentioned nobleman and the Cow Boy ink-slinger.

We went into camp at Ash-coolie at 8:30 after devouring enough grub to feed a regiment, wrapped ourselves in our blankets and by the light of the moon and to the music of a mosquito band, attempted to woo the drowsy god. He wouldn't woo. The mosquitos came without wooing however, and in the morning we carried with us a perfect illustration of the BAD LANDS in the hills and buttes on our neck.

Right here let me stop to say that Joe. Pennell had better seek more congenial climes before we return to Medora. His parting wish that it would rain every day was more than fulfilled. The disguised nobleman was sure Joe. had hoo-dooed us and before we arrived we came to the same conclusion.

Tuesday morning at 3 o'clock we awaked in a drizzling rain. After considerable trouble we got our fire going, boiled and bolted our coffee straight and hot and started on. Had it not been for Mr. Palmer's thoughtfulness in getting a rubber coat we would now be a dead animal by the wayside. It was colder than a defeated candidates reception of his successful competitor and damper tnan the law allows. As the ministsr said: "It was a dam-p cold day." For four hours and a half, until 8 o'clock we rode through the driving rain, when it began to slack, but was cold till 11 o'clock. When 46 1-10 miles from Medora we overtook Lieut. Varnum with his government outfit. After a pleasant chat and an explantion of the odometer by the Lieutenant, we started on and went into camp at Chalk buttes at 11. After dinner we went to sleep and awoke at 1:30 with the rays of the sun shining directly in our upturned faces and the thermometer chassezing up to 130 degrees. Every exposed part of our flesh was "done" "to the queens taste." The mosquitos had also been getting in their work very extensively and the result was a fresh accession of buttes and coolies.

Starting on, we saw many antelope, in fact they abounded the whole way. We put up the 800 yard sight on one and had the satisfaction of seeing it drop. Driving toward it, visions of tender antelope stake filled our mind mixed with the recollection of sundry and divers of Johnson's stories about killing buffalo so far that they had begun to decay before he could reach them. But,

"The beautiful vail is rent in two"

very often. When within fifty yards of the antelope it jumped up and dashed over a butte, making a crack in the atmosphere longer than Mark Twain's jack-rabbit. It was positevily disgusting.

This diversion and several others of a kindred nature delayed us so that we made only fifty miles on Tuesday.

Going into camp at 8 o'clock we made a fire of buffalo chips and then made our bed on them to keep them dry in case of rain.

At three Wednesday morning we were again awaked by a driving rain. This thing was getting monotonous but breakfast was cooked to the tune of college glee songs and we started on in good spirits at four. This was our best day's travelling, amonting to at least seventy-five miles. We made a long stop at the E6 ranch, arriving there just in time to avoid a terrific rain and wind storm. Russ Wilson entertained us royally and after a five hour's stop, we started on, reaching the South Moreau and Macy's ranch at 9:30.
articles.summary: Packard's account of the first days of his buckboard trip from Medora toward the Black Hills: rain, mosquitoes, antelope, Lieut. Varnum's survey party, and stops at the E6 ranch and Macy's ranch on the South Moreau.

articles.text: The first gun has been fired and from now until the close of the campaign in November, the political horizon will be eagerly watched by most of our readers. Billings county, at the coming territorial conventions will be entitled to two delegates and therefore have a voice in matters political, to which its rapid growth and great prosperity so well entitle it. For the first time in the history of trans-Missouri politics, representation will be conceded to this section of the country in the coming legislature and the honor naturally falls upon a citizen of Morton, the senior county. The COW BOY has for some time past carefully weighed the merits of the various candidates already in the field and is glad to find a man in every way qualified to come up to the requirements of the occasion. We refer to Mr. L. N. Cary, of Mandan, of the well-known firm of Carpenter & Cary. This gentleman combines to a large extent the essentials of a valuable legislator and his nomination cannot bnt meet with universal approbation by all thinking people. Mr. Cary is a pioneer of the west Missouri country, thoroughly conversant with the needs and wants of its district, pushing, enterprising and has proven his competency and ability by the phenomenal success achieved in his own business. Mr. Cary is in no sense an office-seeker, never having desired nor held one, but that his services in the legislative halls will be invaluable, is beyond successful contradiction. The COW BOY will have more to say on this subject in its later issues, but simply desires to present its candidate to-day, with the firm belief that no possible candidate possesses in a greater degree than Mr. Cary, the elements needed in our legislator.
articles.summary: Editorial: Billings county will have two delegates at the territorial conventions, and the Cow Boy endorses L. N. Cary of Mandan for the legislature.

articles.text: Reports from all directions are to the effect that cattlemen have awakened to the importance of having plenty of bulls on the range. From the gulf to the northern limit of the range, everywhere, bulls are being turned in by the hundreds, and they are generally of a very fair grade. This will tend to greatly increase the calf crop, and proportionately increase the profits of the business. Let the good work go on. Now if you will keep the bulls up in the winter and spring, and wean your calves in the fall, your cup of success will be nearly full.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped item on cattlemen turning more bulls onto the range.

articles.text: In every flock and herd there will be more or less imperfectly formed or defectively-consituted produce, which, if suffered to perpetuate their defects, will depreciate the value of the breed. These should be thrown out or consigned to the block, and never permitted to breed their kind, to degenerate the blood of their kindred. It is this weeding out practice that has preserved our stock from degenerating. It was by selecting out the most perfect scions to breed from that our stock has been raised to its present high standard of excellence. Grading up is the ladder of promotion; the top round is the summit of perfection.—[Montana Stock and Mining Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped item on culling defective animals from herds.

articles.text: To buy a horse, an intending purchaser should have the horse brought out before him, and watch the animal as he stands at rest. If the owner is continually starting the horse in motion, and urging him to "show off," something may be suspected; because it is when a horse is at perfect rest that his weak points are divulged. If the horse is sound he will stand square on his limbs, without moving any one of them, the feet being placed flat on the ground, and all his legs plump and naturally posed. If one foot be thrown forward, and the weight taken from it, disease or tenderness may be suspected.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped advice on judging a horse before buying.

articles.text: There is a disposition on the part of herd owners to become careless about the ages and condition of their bulls. To begin with, bulls should not be put in the herd until they are twenty months or two years old. If yearlings are placed in the herd it should only be for a short time. After a bull has been two seasons with the herd he should be removed. He is no good for service, and as long as you keep him you will figure him in as one of your active partners in the business. Get rid of him and fill his place with a two-year old. These remarks apply to bulls having the freedom of the range. If you are prepared to take them up in the fall and feed them through the winter, and then hold them apart from the herd until July, they will last a couple of years longer and still be valuable. Then will come the question of in and in breeding. If you are satisfied to indulge in that practice you may hold the bulls in the range for four years. But old bulls are a nuisance, viewed from any range standpoint, and the proper method is to abate them.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped advice on the age and replacement of range bulls.

articles.text: From all parts of Dakota and Montana come reports of the depredations of horse-thieves. We think we are entirely within bounds in stating that in Dakota alone, there have been at least two hundred head stolen, and scarcely more than a half dozen have been recovered. Several men have also been hung for horse-stealing, but the plague still goes on. In South Heart, Sunday evening, four valuable horses were stolen from Mr Morton's barn, and as the trail has been closely followed, we hope that by this time the horses are recovered and the thieves hung. Mr. Lang writes in reference to his stolen horses that the thieves forgot to take the halters, which he will keep for their personal adornment. We wish to be placed on record as believing that the only way to cure horse-stealing is to hang the thief wherever caught. The end, in this case, fully justifies the means.
articles.summary: Editorial on horse-stealing in Dakota and Montana, reporting four horses stolen from Mr. Morton's barn at South Heart on Sunday evening and Mr. Lang's stolen horses.

articles.text: The cattle business, the most important industry of the west, is in some respects peculiar. In no other transactions, save those of handling stock, is so much reliance placed on a man's honor and word. Thousands of dollars are often involved and depend on the honer of a single man. It is therefore highly necessary that all cattle trades be conducted on square business principles. If a man engaged in the business wishes to stand well among his neighbors,he must do exactly as he says he will, without regard to the consequences. We might say that in no other businss is one dependent upon his neighbors for assistance so much as in cattle dealing. When a sale is made, care should be exercised that nothing be misrepresented. The temporary profits will not balance the future harm caused by the loss of a good name. Buyers should understand their business, and not say one thing and mean another. A slight mistake may cause a stock grower much trouble. Ranchmen have the cure in their hands. Let them refuse to have any dealings with those whose business conduct is not "straight," and the crooked gentleman will soon find the field lonely and seek pastures new.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Clipped item on honesty in cattle trading.

articles.text: A company has just been organized in New York for the purpose of operating an inmense ranch in the southwest corner of New Mexico. The company is called the Lyons & Campbell Ranch and Cattle company, and has a capital stock of $1,500,000. The president is John C. Barron, of the United Railroads of New Jersey; vice president, Mr. Oliver Sumner Teall; treasurer, Mr. E. Harrison Sanford, treasurer of the Stampfords Manufacturing company; secretary, Mr. Lester M. Clark; manager, Mr. Thomas Lyons: directors, Mr. John C. Barron, Gen. George B. McClellan, Mr. E. Harrison Sanford, Mr. Thomas Lyons, Mr. A. A. Sumner, Mr. George B. Post, Mr. Brayton Ives, Mr. John J. McCook and Mr. Oliver Sumner. The company's property is a combination of a number of ranches along the Gila river and the streams and springs in that vicinity. The ranches are named as follows: the Caves Springs, the White House, the Buck Horn, the Mule Spring, the Harding Cienega and the Lower of Gila ranch. Their range is about forty miles from east to west and sixty miles from north to south, and comprises over 1,500,000 acres of grazing land, at an altitude of from 3,000 to 6,000 feet. The stock consists of 150 horses, 16,000 head of cattle and 200 thoroughbreds.—[Pioneer Press.
articles.summary: Clipped report on the new Lyons & Campbell Ranch and Cattle company in New Mexico.

articles.text: The attention of our readers is called to the astonishingly liberal campaign offer of the publishers of the Weekly Pioneer Press. It is proposed to send the Weekly Pioneer Press to any address in the United States or Canada, postage prepaid, for eight months for seventy-five cents. To those who are already subscribers to this excellent journal, it is unnecessary for us to extol its merits; but to those who are unfamiliar with its columns we would say that the Weekly Pioneer Press stands at the head and front of journalism in this country. For full and complete news and miscellany, interesting correspondence from all parts of the world, accurate and complete market reports, it is excelled by no weekly paper, East or West. Those subscribing now will receive the paper during the entire presidential campaign and until after the assembling of congress, next fall. We have made a clubbing arrangement which permits us to offer the Weekly Pioneer Press and the BAD LANDS COW BOY for eight months for $2.00, and confidently expect that nearly every man in the county will avail himself of this opportunity to secure their home paper and a first-class metropolitan paper for the small sum above named. This offer will be open until next September, and in order to cover the full campaign, subscriptions should be made at once.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy announces a clubbing offer with the Weekly Pioneer Press: both papers for eight months for $2.00.

articles.text: Lloyd Roberts returned Tuesday morning with several car-loads of Minnesota three-year-old heifers for Wm. Dantz.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts brought in several car-loads of Minnesota heifers for Wm. Dantz.

articles.text: The weather lately has been of unmixed perfection. Sun-shine by day and rain by night has a tendency to make everyone happy.
articles.summary: Fine weather: sun by day, rain by night.

articles.text: The Eatons have moved to their new home ranch at the logging camp, where they will hererfter reside. Messrs. Tarbell and Bond are now living at the Custer Trail ranch.
articles.summary: The Eatons moved to their new home ranch at the logging camp; Tarbell and Bond now live at the Custer Trail ranch.

articles.text: Mr. Gallup, of New York, started for home last Monday. Like every other visitor here, he was firmly convinced that the Bad Lands are destined to be one of the greatest cattle raising sections of the United States. He expects to go into the cattle business himself.
articles.summary: Mr. Gallup of New York left for home, intending to enter the cattle business.

articles.text: Wm. M. Brewer, who has been here for several weeks, left yesterday morning for Bismarck. He will continue on from there to Pierre and thence to his home in Deadwood. "Billy" has made many friends here, but we don't blame him for thinking, "there's no place like home."
articles.summary: Wm. M. Brewer left for Bismarck on his way home to Deadwood.

articles.text: A solitary deer stood for a long time on the butte east of town, Tuesday evening, sharply outlined against the evening sky and doubtless wondering at the great change which had come over its old feeding ground in the last year. It is a wonderful change, and one typical of Medora's future.
articles.summary: A lone deer stood on the butte east of town Tuesday evening.

articles.text: D. K. Wade finished driving the cattle of the LeMoyne cattle company from Glendive to his range on Tepee bottom last Saturday. The trip was made overland by Mr. Wade and he was accompanied by his wife and daughter. The cattle are all high grades and are as good looking a lot as we ever saw.
articles.summary: D. K. Wade finished driving the LeMoyne cattle company herd overland from Glendive to Tepee bottom.

articles.text: One of the quickest jobs we have ever seen, is the building of the new freight house here. A still further force of men was added yesterday and the house will probably be ready for occupancy next week. Then the question as to which town shall be the freighting point, will be brought to a focus immediately. "What will poor Bramble do then."
articles.summary: The new freight house at Medora is nearly done; more men were added yesterday.

articles.text: We are not proud and will walk after this—when our choice is a bucker or no ride. We always thought it very funny to see a bronco buck, but will hereafter watch the wild gyrations with an awe-struck feeling of reverence at the unadulterated cussedness of the brute. It is needless to add that we have been bucked.
articles.summary: The editor reports being thrown by a bucking bronco.

articles.text: About two hundred and fifty teachers from the Madison convention came through here Monday evening, bound for the Yellowstone park and Alaska. The feminine portion of the excursion seemed to have a wonderful curiosity to see some cow-boys and we still have a dark suspicion that some of them were corralled here.
articles.summary: About 250 teachers from the Madison convention passed through Monday evening, bound for Yellowstone and Alaska.

articles.text: The unanimous report of all who have been down the road is that the crops, especially between here and Bismarck, are better than they have ever been. This is illustrated by specimens of wheat, oats and barley brought by Dr. Morton from his father's farm at South Heart and now on exhibition at this office. Specimens of oats also brought from South Heart by R. J. Jewell have double and triple heads eighteen inches long. Like Banquo's ghost, Dakota will not "down."
articles.summary: Crops along the line are excellent; Dr. Morton and R. J. Jewell brought grain specimens from South Heart to the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: Bob Roberts returned Tuesday night from Bismarck, whither he had gone on business. During his absence, he was appointed U. S. commissioner to represent the Bad Lands at the World's fair, to begin at New Orleans next December. No better choice could have been made of commissioner, as Bob has already gone to work gathering petrifactions and other curiosities so numerous in the Bad Lands. Now is the time for each one to step forward and lend a helping hand to lighten the labors of our commissioner. He is thoroughly in earnest about showing the resources and natural curiosities of the Bad Lands to the world and should receive the willing assistance of every one.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts returned from Bismarck, having been appointed U.S. commissioner to represent the Bad Lands at the New Orleans World's Fair.

articles.text: The jolliest party that has yet visited the Bad Lands left last Monday evening for the National park and consisted of Mr. M. C. Eaton, of Irvington, N. Y., a relative of the Eatons here, Major O. H. Stevens, New York city and late master of transportation of the N. P. Yellowstone division and Wm. H. Shurtz, a young attorney of Newark, N. J. The party took in the prominent sights of the Bad Lands and were careful inquirers into the profits of cattle raising. It is their intention to put in a large herd soon. They were all confident of the great future of the Bad Lands and of Medora as a cattle centre. Their confidence in the feasibility of the Medora and Black Hills R. R. was backed by the fact that an abundance of capital could be found to complete it. The impression left by these gentlemen will long be favorably remembered, coupled with a hope for a repetion of the visit.
articles.summary: A visiting party of M. C. Eaton, Major O. H. Stevens and Wm. H. Shurtz left for Yellowstone after touring the Bad Lands and planning to start a herd.

articles.text:
In company with Mr. Gallup, we took a very pleasant ride up the river Sunday. We were hospitably entertained at the Custer Trail ranch by Messrs. Tarbell and Bond and did full justice to Mrs. Lebo's bountiful dinner. At Sloping Bottom ranch we found a jolly company consisting of Mrs. J. L. Roberts and daughters, Misses Ubermann and Friedman and Messrs. Dantz, Friedmar, Tucker and several others. A cavalcade was formed and a ride to Tepee bottom with a pleasant call on Mr. and Mrs. Wade made an agreeable stopping point. The onward journey was through the Prairie-dog bottom and the saucy pertness of its ten thousand inhabitants was as comical as ever. Our journey's end was reached at Will Dantz' ranch, the unanimous opinion being that it was too pleasant and prosperous a home for Will to "bach" it any longer. On the return trip, Mrs. Roberts' "bread and milk supper" was found to consist of all the luxuries of the season and we continued our homeward journey at peace with all mankind.

[Since putting the above in type, we have learned that quite a serious loss has befallen Mr. Dantz. Tuesday, the river was very high and while crossing below Ferris & Merrifield's, the team became entangled in the harness and one was drowned almost immediately, the other dying soon afterward. During the struggle to release the horses, Will himself became entangled in the harness, and it was only by great good luck that he escaped drowning.]
articles.summary: Packard's Sunday ride up the Little Missouri with Mr. Gallup to the Custer Trail, Sloping Bottom, Wade and Dantz ranches; postscript reports Will Dantz's team drowned Tuesday crossing the river below Ferris & Merrifield's.
